title: How Many Thrones Did John See in Heaven?
batchLabel: God Is One / One Throne
claim: John saw a throne set in heaven, and one sat on it. In the last chapter, the throne of God and of the Lamb is one throne, with one face and one name, not two seats side by side.
objection: "The throne of God and of the Lamb means two divine persons on two thrones, or two figures sharing a court."
answer: Read the wording all the way through. Revelation 22:3–4 uses singular pronouns: "his servants shall serve him," "they shall see his face," "his name shall be in their foreheads." The Lamb is not given a second throne. Walk the passages in order and let the grammar lead.

title: Is There Any God Beside the LORD?
batchLabel: God Is One / One Throne
claim: The LORD excludes any divine being beside himself. He is the first and the last, and no God was formed before Him or after Him. In Revelation, Jesus takes the same first-and-last title and then signs the letter with His own name.
objection: "Isaiah is only denying other idols, not denying distinct divine persons."
answer: Isaiah 43:10 goes further than idols: "before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me." Isaiah 44:6 adds, "beside me there is no God." The same speaker is the first and the last. When Jesus says "the first and the last" and signs it, "I Jesus," the passages belong to one identity, not a second God standing beside the LORD.

title: Is the Holy Ghost Another Person Beside the Father?
batchLabel: God Is One / One Throne
claim: The Holy Ghost is God's own Spirit in holy action and presence, not another divine Spirit alongside the Father. Scripture moves between Spirit of God, Spirit of the Father, Spirit of Christ, and Holy Ghost because one Spirit is being described.
objection: "Jesus promised 'another Comforter,' so the Holy Ghost must be another person beside the Father and beside Jesus."
answer: Keep reading. In the same conversation Jesus says, "I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you" (John 14:18). Paul describes the same indwelling presence as the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ (Romans 8:9–11). Matthew 10:20 calls that speaking presence "the Spirit of your Father." The distinction is functional: Holy Ghost names God as He moves, fills, sanctifies, speaks, and dwells in believers.

title: Does the Bible Actually Call Jesus God?
batchLabel: Jesus Is God / the Father in the Son
claim: Yes. Scripture identifies Jesus as God while also presenting Him as genuinely human for our salvation. John calls the Word God. Thomas addresses the risen Jesus as "My Lord and my God." Hebrews addresses the Son as God.
objection: "Those verses only mean Jesus is a divine agent, or that He represents God, not that He is God."
answer: The site's case does not rest on one isolated phrase. John says the Word was God and later says the Word was made flesh. Thomas speaks to the risen Jesus, not past Him. Hebrews applies the title God directly to the Son. Read together, these passages identify Jesus within the divine identity, while the same New Testament also presents His genuine humanity. Human experiences such as hunger, prayer, and death do not cancel that identity.

title: Why Does All the Fulness Dwell in Him?
batchLabel: Jesus Is God / the Father in the Son
claim: Colossians 2:9 means that all the fulness of deity dwells bodily in Jesus Christ. God is not partially present in Christ; the one God is fully revealed and dwelling in Him in genuine humanity. Paul does not describe Jesus as containing one part of God.
objection: "If the Godhead is three persons, 'all the fulness' only means the fullness of one of those persons, or a share of divine qualities."
answer: The language is total: *all* the fulness of the Godhead, *bodily*, in Him. Colossians 1:19 says the same with "all fulness." John 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:19 belong to that pattern: the Father dwelling in Him does the works, and God was in Christ reconciling the world unto Himself. Nothing in the wording suggests a third, a remainder, or a divided Godhead.

title: Is Jesus the Father?
batchLabel: Jesus Is God / the Father in the Son
claim: Jesus is not the Father as to His humanity as the Son, yet the Father is fully revealed and dwelling in Him. The Bible preserves the Father and Son distinction without presenting two Gods or two divine Spirits.
objection: "If you say Jesus is God, you must be saying Jesus is the Father, and that erases the Son. Or, on the other side: Isaiah 9:6 cannot call the child 'The everlasting Father' without confusion."
answer: Use Jesus' own explanation. He answers Philip's request to see the Father by pointing to Himself, then immediately explains: the Father dwells in Him and does the works. The Father is not a second visible divine being standing beside Jesus. The Son is the man Christ Jesus, born of Mary, who lived in real relation to God. Isaiah 9:6 places divine titles, including Mighty God and Everlasting Father, on the child who would be born. The child is born in time; the God revealed in Him is everlasting.

title: What Does "the Word Was Made Flesh" Mean?
batchLabel: The Word Became Flesh / the Son of God
claim: God's eternal self-expression became flesh, not a second God beside Him. The eternal Word belongs to God's own identity and is God, and that Word entered genuine human existence.
objection: "'The Word was with God, and the Word was God' means two divine persons, one with the other from eternity."
answer: John 1 is not introducing a second God. The Word is God's own eternal self-expression: the Word was God, all things were made by Him, and the Word was made flesh. The article *John 1 and Genesis 1* reads John's opening as the one Creator's Word becoming flesh. "With God" does not require a second divine being standing beside the one God who created alone (see Episode 12).

title: Did the Son Exist Eternally?
batchLabel: The Word Became Flesh / the Son of God
claim: The one who became the Son is eternally God, but Scripture connects sonship to the incarnation, birth, and redemptive mission. Jesus did not begin to exist at Bethlehem. The divine identity revealed in Him is eternal. Sonship describes the incarnate life brought forth in time.
objection: "If Jesus is God, the Son must have existed eternally as a second person, or else you are denying His deity."
answer: Distinguish identity from role, and let Scripture choose the terms. The Bible explicitly calls the Word eternal and explicitly says the Son was born, given, made of a woman, and sent in the likeness of sinful flesh. The title "Son of God" is tied, in Luke 1:35, to what happened in Mary's womb. Denying an eternal Son as a second divine being is not the same as saying Jesus began to exist at Bethlehem.

title: Why Is Jesus Called the Son of God?
batchLabel: The Word Became Flesh / the Son of God
claim: Jesus is called the Son of God because He was conceived by the Holy Ghost and born of Mary as the holy human manifestation through whom God saved us. Luke gives the cause: the angel says "therefore" the holy thing born would be called the Son of God. The title is tied to what happened in Mary's womb. "Son" does not mean lesser deity. The Son is the image of the invisible God and the bodily dwelling of all divine fulness.
objection: "'Son of God' means a lesser divine being, begotten in eternity as a second person."
answer: Luke 1:35 will not bear that reading. The angel ties the title to conception and birth with a "therefore." Matthew adds that the child conceived by the Holy Ghost is Emmanuel, "God with us." Sonship is not a reduced deity. It is the genuine human life of Jesus Christ, in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily.

title: Why Did Jesus Pray If He Is God?
batchLabel: Why Jesus Prayed / the Right Hand of God
claim: Jesus prayed from His genuine human life as the Son, not because a second divine God needed help from the first. Prayer proves the incarnation was real. It does not prove that God is divided into multiple divine centers.
objection: "If Jesus is God, He would not need to pray. Prayer is proof of two divine persons, one speaking to the other."
answer: Hebrews 5:7 places the prayers "in the days of his flesh." Gethsemane shows a real human will submitted to God, not a staged conversation: "not my will, but thine, be done." The same Gospel that records Jesus praying also records Him saying the Father dwelt in Him and that whoever saw Him saw the Father. Read the prayers through the incarnation. The distinction is real because the humanity is real. It is not proof of two divine beings.

title: Who Was Jesus Praying To?
batchLabel: Why Jesus Prayed / the Right Hand of God
claim: The man Christ Jesus prayed to the eternal God who was His Father and who also dwelt in Him. As man, Jesus possessed a human will, human consciousness, and genuine dependence. His prayers were not staged conversations. The Father was not absent from Christ while receiving Christ's prayers.
objection: "Prayer requires one person talking to another person, so the Father and the Son must be two divine persons."
answer: The incarnate Son lived a real human relationship to God. That is why He prayed. One God remained indivisible: Jesus said the Father was in Him doing the works. Distinguish the praying man Christ Jesus from the eternal God without creating two Gods. The relationship is true because the humanity is true.

title: Does the Right Hand Mean a Second Throne?
batchLabel: Why Jesus Prayed / the Right Hand of God
claim: The right hand of God means divine power, authority, victory, honor, and exalted rule. When Scripture places Jesus at God's right hand, it describes the Messiah's supreme authority rather than a second divine body seated beside God. The right hand is biblical authority and exaltation language, not a second throne beside God.
objection: "Stephen saw Jesus standing on the right hand of God, so there must be two divine persons side by side, and two thrones."
answer: Let Scripture define its own symbol first. Before any ascension passage, the LORD's right hand dashes enemies and is exalted. These are not descriptions of a literal divine limb. Psalm 110:1 is royal language: the Messiah receives authority while enemies are made His footstool. Stephen's vision is a real vision of the exalted Son and the glory of God; a vision can communicate that distinction without turning God's right hand into anatomy or adding a second throne. Peter, on Pentecost, reads the same language as exaltation: God has made that same Jesus both Lord and Christ.

title: Does 1 Corinthians 15 Mean Jesus Stops Existing?
batchLabel: Why Jesus Prayed / the Right Hand of God
claim: No. The passage describes the completion of redemptive administration, not the erasure of Jesus Christ. The mediatorial kingdom and subjection of the Son reach their goal, but the risen Jesus remains the visible revelation of God. The role reaches fulfillment; the risen Christ is not annihilated.
objection: "'Then shall the Son also himself be subject' means the Son ceases, is absorbed, or stops existing when God is all in all."
answer: What ends is the mediatorial reign over enemies, once death is destroyed. What remains is the glorified Lamb and the eternal high priest. Hebrews 7:24 says this man "continueth ever" and has an unchangeable priesthood. Revelation 22 still shows the throne of God and of the Lamb, with one face and one name, after every enemy is gone. The Son's saving administration reaches its appointed goal. The risen Jesus does not disappear.

title: Why Did the Apostles Baptize in Jesus' Name?
batchLabel: The Name of Jesus / Baptism in Jesus' Name
claim: The apostles baptized in Jesus' name because Jesus is the saving name given under heaven, and baptism identifies the believer with His death, burial, and resurrection. Every explicit baptismal naming recorded after the resurrection points to Jesus Christ or the Lord Jesus. Jews, Samaritans, Gentiles, and disciples of John were directed into the same name.
objection: "Those verses only mean baptism was done by Jesus' authority, so the spoken name does not matter, and Matthew 28:19 is the real formula."
answer: Authority is part of the phrase, but Acts does not use authority as a reason to remove Jesus' name from baptism. The inspired record repeatedly connects the baptism itself with the name of Jesus Christ or the Lord Jesus, across every kind of audience. (Episode 20 takes this objection head on. Episode 18 reads Matthew 28:19 with Acts rather than against it.)

title: Why the Apostles Used the Name
batchLabel: The Name of Jesus / Baptism in Jesus' Name
claim: No, Matthew 28:19 does not contradict Acts 2:38. Matthew commands baptism in the singular name, and Acts records the apostles invoking that name as Jesus Christ. As the site puts it: Matthew gives the command. Luke identifies the saving name. Acts records the execution.
objection: "Matthew 28:19 is the baptismal formula Jesus gave, so Acts 2:38 is a contradiction, a later change, or only a shorthand for authority."
answer: The command says "name," singular, before naming Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. That wording invites the reader to ask what name is being revealed. Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are revelatory titles. Luke 24 is the bridge: the risen Jesus commands that repentance and remission of sins be preached in His name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. Acts 2 is that Jerusalem beginning. Every later named baptism in Acts stays with Jesus Christ or the Lord Jesus. The passages should be read as one commission, not as competing formulas.

title: Is There Any Other Name Whereby We Must Be Saved?
batchLabel: The Name of Jesus / Baptism in Jesus' Name
claim: Jesus is the revealed saving name proclaimed and invoked by the apostles. There is no other name under heaven given among men whereby we must be saved. The name given at birth already means He shall save His people from their sins, and that name is exalted above every name.
objection: "The saving 'name' is a general reference to Jesus' authority or reputation, not a name to be preached, believed, and invoked in baptism."
answer: Matthew 1:21 gives the name because He shall save His people. Acts 4:12 says there is none other name given among men whereby we must be saved. Apostolic preaching consistently centers salvation, remission of sins, authority, and baptism in the name of Jesus Christ. A biblical name carries identity and authority together. title: Does "In the Name" Mean Authority Only?
batchLabel: The Name of Jesus / Baptism in Jesus' Name
claim: "In the name of Jesus" includes authority, but it is not only an unspoken idea of authority. Baptism is into Christ, into His death, and into the name in which salvation is found. Acts 22:16 joins baptism with calling on the name of the Lord. Faith, invocation, identification with Christ, and obedience belong together.
objection: "'In the name of Jesus' is just an idiom for 'by His authority,' so a person may be baptized with other words, or with no spoken name at all, and still obey the New Testament."
answer: Authority is part of the phrase. The Acts passages, however, do not make authority a reason to remove Jesus' name from baptism. The same record keeps connecting the baptism itself with the name of Jesus Christ or the Lord Jesus. Acts 22:16 strengthens the connection by joining baptism with calling on the name of the Lord. The name is not a magical formula detached from faith, and it is not reduced to an unspoken idea. Romans 6 shows the same center: baptism into Jesus Christ, into His death, buried with Him.

title: What Did Jesus Mean by Water and the Spirit?
batchLabel: The New Birth / the Holy Ghost, with tongues as the initial sign
claim: The apostolic response to the gospel includes repentance, water baptism, and receiving the Holy Ghost. John 3 and Acts 2 are read as one salvation message. Jesus teaches a new birth involving water and Spirit. When the first hearers after the resurrection asked, "What shall we do?", the apostolic answer was repentance, baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, and the promise of the Holy Ghost.

answer: Jesus is answering a question about entering the kingdom, and He names water and the Spirit together. The first post-resurrection gospel appeal in Acts receives a response that also joins water and the Spirit: baptism in Jesus' name and the gift of the Holy Ghost, beginning with repentance. The site reads those passages as one message, not two religions. The pathways *The New Birth* and *The Gospel Pattern* walk that connection in order.

The thief is not a loophole in a command that had not yet been given.

title: Is Tongues the Initial Sign of the Holy Ghost?
batchLabel: The New Birth / the Holy Ghost, with tongues as the initial sign
claim: In Acts, the repeated sign that the Holy Ghost had been received was speaking with other tongues. This is seen at the beginning in Jerusalem (Acts 2:4), among the Gentiles (Acts 10:44–46), and at Ephesus (Acts 19:6). Peter later calls the Gentile outpouring "the like gift" and "as on us at the beginning" (Acts 11:15–17). That reception sign in Acts is not the same question as the public gift in 1 Corinthians 12:30.
objection: "1 Corinthians 12:30 asks, 'do all speak with tongues?', so tongues cannot be the initial sign for every believer; it is only a gift for some."
answer: Keep the two passages in their own arguments. Acts is recording people receiving the Holy Ghost for the first time, and the sign that convinced Jewish believers in Acts 10 was that "they heard them speak with tongues." Paul, in 1 Corinthians 12, is correcting the public use of gifts in a church that already had the Spirit. The pathway *Tongues as the Initial Sign* is built on that distinction: the repeated reception sign in Acts is not cancelled by the later question about the public gift. Read Acts 2, 10, and 19 first, then read Corinthians in that light.
